game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

Well, that was interesting and certainly thought provoking. 

It's basically read things, listen to calls, spy on computers/phones, drag'n'drop info into a file, connect the dots, profile people... solve the crime, maybe even save the world, all the while being the faceless investigator behind a remote screen of a computer. Various endings based on your skill and decisions.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Big Brother watches you. That’s what they told us back in the days, when it was just some kinda fiction and a fantastic story. Now, in our present times this issue has become like a real problem, especially for someone who believes, that their lives are important as hell and like to play a private card all the time. 

The government can learn about you literally everything, thanks to social media, your online purchases, all the cameras hanging around the city, watching at you, information you provide to your employers when you attend to job, mobile phones you use with a GPS modules, etc. 

It can be a problem for lots of people, especially for some who is paranoid and doesn’t seem to be busy all the time with any kind of work (because, otherwise, they wouldn’t have time for these kind of thoughts). On the other hand, it can be really helpful to identify a threat and prevent some kind of tragedy from a single murder to a massive terrorist attack.

Orwell try to develop this idea. In this game, which presents as a visual novel with its own dystopia universe, you have to identify the threat. You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life.

So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions.

And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed.

At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. 

Orwell is definitely a blast. It has this unique kind of a gameplay with its deep idea and rich stories for someone, who truly values games as a real art. The combination of twists, turnabouts and all these thrilling moments make this game a great place to spend a few hours, maybe dozens of hours, if you will feel like having more than one run to reveal all the achievements and endings. 

Okay, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:

+ Conspiracy theory lover
+ Love the idea of investigating and matching data and clues into one piece 
+ You want to entertain yourself in a great story game for at least few hours
+ Like to dig to the bottom to find out who is who
+ Fan of dramatic stories with its twists, thrilling moments and surprises

Recommend to avoid if you:

- Don’t get the idea of visual novel
- Not a fan of all these talks that government spy on you and we are all under control.  

Enjoy!

You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life. So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions. And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed. At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. Orwell is definitely a blast. It has this unique kind of a gameplay with its deep idea and rich stories for someone, who truly values games as a real art. The combination of twists, turnabouts and all these thrilling moments make this game a great place to spend a few hours, maybe dozens of hours, if you will feel like having more than one run to reveal all the achievements and endings. Okay, to sum everything up! You should grab this game if you: + Conspiracy theory lover + Love the idea of investigating and matching data and clues into one piece + You want to entertain yourself in a great story game for at least few hours + Like to dig to the bottom to find out who is who + Fan of dramatic stories with its twists, thrilling moments and surprises Recommend to avoid if you: - Don’t get the idea of visual novel - Not a fan of all these talks that government spy on you and we are all under control. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Great game, I got it in the humble bundle monthly along with other games, and decided to play it because it looked interesting.

Describing the game, it's a very well made point and click adventure, but it's different from your typical point and click games because here you just use Orwell, an operating system designed to watch and monitor people, you can browse different websites and access all sorts of public and private information about your suspects, you go from page to page, phone to phone, computer to computer, device to device, as you try and look for useful information that may help you in your objectives.

The story is short but entertaining and exciting, you get the feeling of really becoming an Orwell 'investigator', the feeling is authentic, the websites, pages, profiles, articles, and that sort of stuff seemed believable enough to get you going into the story. Sometimes the story feels a little bit linear and forced upon you, e.g. pages that you need to look into for information will sometimes be spoonfed to you. but I get it though, if it wasn't though, many people won't know what to do next and get stuck, and they will need to add a lot more useless filler pages/information to make it a more realistic and harder experience. As typical with these kinds of games, there are multiple endings, all affected by your choices in the game. so it adds a bit of replay value.

I only hope they add more episodes/cases next, as the story is a bit short and there is potential for more storytelling using the Orwell system, I also hope they added in voice acting for the voice call tapping parts. so It feels even more authentic. 

I'd also not recommend it for it's full price at the moment(IF they add in more free episodes/cases, then I will change my stance about this, a Season Two is coming though, but that's for another price unfortunately). if you can get it for 50% off, I'd say it's now worth it. For me, I got it in a humble bundle monthly subscription that gives around $200 worth of good games for around $12 a month, along with Rise of the Tomb Raider and other more games.

Score: 7/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Believable writing and gameplay mesh to bring the Orwellian nightmare to life.[/b]

[u][i]Summary:[/i][/u]
With [i]Orwell[/i] literally simulating a job, its success or failure as a game almost entirely hinges on the strength of its writing. Fortunately for all of us, it succeeds with flying colors. The characters it depicts are distinct and memorable. The scenarios it presents to you demand your full attention, else you miss something that leads to catastrophe. In the end it will leave you wondering how else things could have played out.

To be clear, [i]Orwell[/i] is an almost entirely text based experience. It mimics a work computer, including internet browser, email, and even a news and weather report. There is no voice acting, though the voice in my head for each of them is so strong that I had to pause and double check myself on that. Props again to the writers for that. The sound in the game sets a good atmosphere but is limited in quantity to the point of being noticeably repetitive.

If you can stomach the reading load, [i]Orwell[/i] is a novel game that is well worth your time and the cost of admission.

[u][i]Additional details:[/i][/u]
The visual style of [i]Orwell[/i] does an excellent job of being familiar enough to reality while also smoothing over reality's rough edges and mismatching designs. Throughout the game you'll uncover multiple pictures of the same character, often showing different sides of the person than you've seen before. For example you may first discover a finely manicured business photo before later discovering a photo of the same person out on the town, presumably a few drinks in and having a good time. Of course these aren't real photos, but artist renditions.

In order to discuss this next topic, I'll give you the most basic, spoiler free description of what you do in the game. You are tasked with investigating specific people and deciding whether what you find does or does not get added to a government database. Essentially you are both the spy and the filter between your target and the government. With that said, there were a few instances related to this that hampered my immersion. Generally it came from being required to enter a piece of information into the Big Brother system that I would have elected to keep private had it not been needed to progress.

I'll close with a few words on replayability. While there are multiple endings and outcomes to each chapter, I personally didn't feel compelled to replay more than a couple specific moments. The decisions that lead to each result are rarely obvious, so it's hard to go back and change things without reexamining things on a larger scale than I was interested in. There are guides out there that could speed up the process if you're so interested. I happily spent 9 hours with [i]Orwell[/i], nearly all of which was a single careful playthrough.

review_text_raw:
PROS: I highly recommend everyone to play the DEMO of this game first. It'll give you a great feel of how the entire game is going to go, so you will know if you will like it or not. I'm going to be honest, this is not my normal type of game. After playing the DEMO, I wanted more of it ASAP. This is great for those who want mystery, political nightmares, and creep-factors. It's also a complete mind-screw as well, which was awesome. The soundtrack was very nice to listen to as well, and it's a smooth transitioning game with a great save-as-you-go feature.  It also has great replay value, so that you can get various outcomes.

CONS: I bought the game and flew through threw the chapters quickly. It's 5 Chapters and it takes about 4 hours to complete all chapters, if you take your time. 4 hours for a 10 dollar game is a bit steep for me. I usually like to get $1 for every hour of playtime, so the game pretty much pays for itself. Although there is replay value to this game, I still don't like how quickly it goes by. The game was also a bit slow and laggy in some spots, like moving datachunks while text was still steaming. 

Overall it's a great quick game, but I would recommend searching for it on sale, and I would also recommend DEMOing the game first. It's definitely not a game made for everyone, but it's got a lot of good going for it!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is only getting more relevant in the years since it’s release given it’s subject matter of government surveillance. It is kind of a visual novel puzzle game where you navigate different platforms finding bits of info that you can tag to the database which in turn can find you more info. As you go on you start to unravel a story of who was behind the bombings. The bits of info are highlighted so you can’t miss them and you also don’t always have to tag them. This is because some info is out of context. For instance someone saying that they are being tortured by cupcakes is obviously not actual torture but you can still tag the person involved as a torturer. Having the discretion is nice but there are other times where you have to tag certain data to progress that I don’t feel was data that must have been tagged or as relevant as the game made it. I also don’t like how you can’t untag data. I also felt that at the end of the game there was supposed to be multiple ways to handle the outcome but I could only see one or possibly two. I don’t know why the other ways weren’t available to me as I can’t think of a story reason that I shouldn’t have been able to pull off what i wanted. The story was good but the twists near the end were simply fantastic. The UI for the game was easy to get used to and had a good design. I also liked how new parts of the software were revealed as they became needed. The game has no voice acting but that wasn’t an issue wand made sense given the fact that outside of recorded calls this was all  just you at a computer. The puzzle aspect was that you have to scour the various blogs; calls; emails; etc to find info you can use to further the game as well as provide additional depth details and context. 

	I played Orwell on Linux. It froze on me once but other than that I encountered no issues and noticed no spelling errors. There are no graphics options and the game has a 60 FPS cap. You can save on exit but there is just one save slot so you can’t undo choices or have multiple save files. Performance was good with no noticeable lag. Alt-Tab Didn’t work.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wrote this review after 3 episodes, I might change it later.

Orwell is an interesting game about collecting personal data from people through various means (social media, dating sites, phone calls etc.) and investigating to find the terrorist/s that plant bombs in public places. The gameplay reminds me a lot of Analogue : Hate Story, which is a good sign. Every document gives you new informations, that leads you to new documents etc.

Overall the writing is very solid and believable, you can only see typed messages but they all express the character's personality : the lawyer is writing slowly with perfect punctuation, the young activist uses slang and typos etc. Sometimes there are some blatant shortcuts designed for exposition (a conversation with an unknown person that starts with "What can I do for you, Susan Mills, my best friend from Hugand University ?") but it didn't bother me too much.

What bothers me however is how much the game holds your hand. You can only select a few informations and only about the suspect "du jour". Several times I thought "Wow, Alan is very suspect !" but I couldn't get any informations about him until the next day where I'm told "Today we'll focus on Alan, he's suspect". Am I the investigator or just a goddamn clerk ?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]What Orwell is[/h1]

This is likely the first thing you might ask yourself if you're considering buying this game. Basically Orwell is a visual novel. The main way the game communicates is through text and the way you progress the story is by character dialogue. The way you trigger the dialogue is the unusual part. Basically you're a government employee whose job is to spy on people and while you do it by reading their e-mails, browsing their facebook page you're highlighted info you might want to add to the government's archive and investigate it. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]

The way the characters unfold is pulled off incredibly well. Despite me being quite the cynical person the game affected me too when I learned about the people's secrets and their motivations behind their actions. I'm being purposefully vague as I don't want to spoil anything. The art style is also quite unique, albeit it's explained poorly (viewing the world through chunks of data and all that). Another plus is that the game is all text so you could run it on anything. I'm sure an android port would be a piece of cake, and you could also play it on your grandma's chromebook.

[h1]The not-so-good[/h1]

The budget constraints were clear as day to me. The phone calls were all text so they weren't any different from the chat conversations, which broke immersion to me. Some voice acting would have elevated things a lot. Another minus is the way the narrative is presented at times. The character archetypes (hacker, government official, shy girl, punk kid) were really stereotypical and made the otherwise heavy dystopian story feel juvenile and borderline teen comedy-esque. The political commentary seemed really black and white, "good guys vs. bad guys" type of story. All the government officials act incredibly arrogant, almost like cartoon villains and all the civilian characters, as stated above, are just plain archetypes (with a few exceptions). So the game could have done a little better in the writing department.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

Orwell is a great visual novel game with a twist, that suffers from a lack of scale (likely due to a limited budget) and some writing flaws, but is overall superb for what it is. Definitely recommended, just don't expect the best game you've ever played.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The dystopian future is upon us. In it, we are tasked with examining all the various data about the target person - their communication, medical reports, posts on social sites, etc.; as all of the information can help us in protecting The Nation and its citizens.
When terror strikes in the heart of the capital, the [i]Orwell[/i] and we with it are put on the front line. With only one suspect at the beginning, we need to search throughout their data for any possible hints that could lead us to the truth about the attacks and the culprits behind them. But more suspects mean more information to get lost in and recognizing what info is relevant will put our deduction skills to a challenge. Also, anything inserted into [i]Orwell[/i] can't be taken back, and even the smallest information can cause a disaster.

Be prepared to read a lot in this game - there is tons of information and every new connection will add more to the ever-growing pile. You don't have to read everything if you don't feel like it, but if you do, you will know more. Simple as that. It can be quite enjoyable to peek into what people share about them on the internet… not very ethical from me, but when else would I have the opportunity? :P
The interface is simple - we are operating in a program that allows us to browse the internet, listen to phone conversations or control a suspect's PC/phone. From all of the information we pick up interesting data and attach it to the respective person. Some data will open new information sources, some are irrelevant or completely wrong, and some are in conflict with each other - from those we need to select the one we deem to be right. Those are the important ones that will influence how the story progress.

What bothered me was the fact that the phone calls can't be skipped or hastened in any way. So other runs for the remaining achievements were a little bit painful. Also, the replayability is somehow dubious - you can take a different approach and frame someone else, but otherwise it's still the same - you need to go through the same talks, lines, everything.

Although I am not much into political stuff and this is full of political talks, I have rather enjoyed it. Through Orwell you can firsthand experience how easily can information be twisted around… not that we don't know already in this age, right?

[hr][/hr]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Duration: Just under 5 hours. 

Orwell is a very unique game.  The player takes the persona of an investigator in a futuristic 1984-style society and tries to find information/evidence regarding some terrorist bombings.  There are 5 chapters in the game which take you on a journey.  The first chapter you are closely led by your examiner, but then more and more choices are laid before you as you delve into websites, eavesdrop on phone calls and investigate hard drives.  

The game is somewhat linear and the main choice is to choose if information is relevant or not to the case and avoiding taking things out of context.  For once you claim something is true, it is stuck in stone.  

Overall, playing Orwell (after the first 60 minutes) became a highly engrossing experience.  The delivery is very well done and even builds to a massive tension where getting information at one point is almost frantic as you are listening to a phone call.  I won't give the details away, but it was tense and somewhat chilling conclusion.  

Overall, a very unique game, full of reading text, but well-delivered. 

7/10 Recommended.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Interactive story hidden behind a simple detective game [/h1]

While the game's premise sounds pretty interesting, the gameplay is quite simple. You read various things such as Internet pages (forums, bank account extract, company's webpage, etc), chat discussions,  listen to live calls which are transcribed and some parts of the text will be highlighted which you can then drag and drop to [b]Orwell[/b], a database which unlocks additional things if a link can be established with the information you've taken.
For a non-spoiler example: you search a person's personal blog and you can find and analyze their username which can then be linked to another forum where it's used for more juicy contents.

It's a bit like [u]A Lost Phone[/u] but its puzzles are MUCH simpler and you can't really get stuck for too long as there's plenty of helpful indicators. Actually, the best part of the game where I really concentrated was when the amount of datachunks (highlighted parts of data in texts) you could import was limited. This really made you think if a [strike]favorite color[/strike] hobby such as artist is a valuable piece of data or not (you could be redirected to an artist page showing past gigs/locations or a contact phone number!).

The best part of the game is the story, because in the end, there's a story and it's told little by little, there are some interesting plot parts (Sorry won't spoil anything) and even if the gameplay sounds boring, the pace is really good and I didn't see time pass by while I finished the 5 episodes. It takes a little bit more than one hour per episode, maybe faster if you just drag and drop without reading.
Even if having a [i]know it all[/i] tool, there are plenty of mysteries to uncover and discovering bit by bit the personalities and relationships of the people you [strike]spy on[/strike] is pretty addictive.

The presentation is pretty nice with its stylish interface. Graphics isn't the most important part of the game but it's good that it's pleasing to the eyes. The music does also its job, it changes when there's a [b]gasp[/b] moment. 

In summary, I recommend this game if you like simple but well told story in a different way than just watching Netflix. It has a nice conspiracy/detective vibe and getting to the finish is an entertaining (and bumpy) ride.
I have definitely put the season 2 on my wishlist!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b] Orwell [/b]

First of, the game "Orwell" is based on the worldwidly popular novel "1984" by George Orwell, whose surname was picked as the game title and which is set in a totalitarian surveillance state. The game is one of the few games that are being released these days that feature unique gameplay and new ideas, although it's not as popular as it would deserve to be. I, however, bought this game during a recent Steam Sale because it struck my eye and I was interested in this.

[h1] What is Orwell and how does it work you ask? [/h1]

Well, in general, "Orwell" is a game where you're supposed to stop crimes with the use of the new software called "Orwell" in a world that is set in our present. You were the chosen one for the new job as a government agent, alone and in charge of "Orwell". Your only direct communication is "Sykes", another agent speaking to you over a one-way-channel and evaluating your actions and decisions. At first, you're being introduced by a short cutscene about an incident that has just happened: a bombing. Now, your task as an anti-crime agent is to find out who committed the crime and later on arrest him or her. At first, you as the "Orwell"-Agent can observe target people (you start with one that was quite obvious in the opening) with the help of 3 programs: the Reader, something to browse news and websites with, the Listener, to eavesdrop on target people once you've collected their number, and finally the Insider, where you can actively browse through the target's personal computer, once again if you collected a certain data. At first you should be browsing through their "Timelines", a website that is similar to social media that we have, e.g. Facebook and Twitter, collecting basic information of them, something like their name, address, birth date and so on. These information are "datachunks" that you can upload to "Orwell" to fill out the targets profile, but you must be careful, as you will not be able to remove data once uploaded. You will get to know your target pretty fast pretty soon as you can observe everything they do online. Later on, there will be so-called "conflicting datachunks", which include at least 2 datachunks. If you choose one datachunk out of the conflicting pair and upload it, the other datachunk will be disabled, so you have to choose wisely once again. If you've done everything right and chose after your liking you will soon arrest your first suspect, great job! After successfully managing a day, you "log off" of "Orwell" and end your day, your work is over for today. As you progress through the episodes, you'll quickly realize how complicated your "first tutorial task" in your new job get and how everything is connected to each other, but I don't want to spoil all your fun.

"Orwell" features 5 episodes for one price in total, releasing 1 each week, and as of 11/11/2016, 4 episodes are already out.

[h1] Do I like it? [/h1]

I definitely do. It's not a very gameplay intensive game, but rather a point and click/drag game, with a bit of thinking involved, however, I think it's very relaxing and it features a packing story. Although, to fully understand the story you have to read everything you find, or you will only get half of the story, which is why I usually need around 90 mins for a full episode, decision making included. The game devs had a really great idea for a new video game and it's almost a bit frightening to decide, whether a person is guilty or not, only based on online data and the game also once again brings up the controversy about surveillance by the government, even in the most private sectors. I mean, you can read what they write to their closest friends and listen to their phone calls. Nonetheless, it's a very innovative game that I really enjoyed, also the soundtrack of the game fits the situation very well and overall, for a 10$ game, "Orwell" is a master piece. I really hope they release a second part of the game or more episodes.

I definitely RECOMMEND the game, and if you're still a bit unsure, you can still try the demo and see for yourself, before you make a decision.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I honestly didn't think this game would absorb me as much as it did.

Orwell is basically a distopian novel played out in the role of an government investigator that's tracking who's behind "The Nation" security, watching out for terrorist activities. You gather information, listen to conversations, spy on devices and find incriminating evidence.

I think the social commentary that the game creates surrounding the use of technology and social media as a gateway to keep track of every single citizen and how easy it is to either be tracked or be impersonated is amazing. We really don't have a great concept of just how much info we voluntarily give to the web, how every single action that we do remains like an unerasable stain floating in the net.

The gameplay is pretty bland, but despite that, I just couldn't get my mind out from the story. It's engaging, entangling, immersive and so well written that I just kept on going and going and going. There's A HUGE LOT of reading to do that's for sure, but it's made in a way that incites the player to keep reading, to uncover every single truth out there, behind the ever-looking eye of the "Big Brother"

I absolutely loved how this also turns around the whole concept of George Orwell's 1984 in a modernized, updated and completely realistic setting. We don't have to keep on imagining and wondering how a society under eternal surveillance looks like. We are already living it.

Definitely loved everything about this game.

Review posted after completing the game. I played the first episode as the Demo, so my hours played may seem anemic.

So, Orwell is a game exploring the concept of an advanced digital surveilance system and it's implications. Gameplay takes the form of what essentially boils down to directed document research. Anyone who played Analogue: A Hate Story will feel right at home. Its usually more exciting than it sounds. As a History graduate, I felt a little nostalgia for my University days.

A game like this lives or dies on its writing, and what is here is pretty high quality. There is the occassional typo but the central characters all speak with their own clearly distinct voices and overall I have nothing but praise for the prose. It explores its themes intelligently without forcing the player into a single interpretation of events. The last episode in particular does clever things with allowing the player to express how they feel about the characters' actions and the Orwell system as a whole.

The music is nice, but limited. The track that plays on twists is a nice touch. No voice acting, but documents don't speak.

I recommend this game to anyone who doesnt mind some reading and is interested in the dilemma around modern mass surveilance.

I don't have a lot of games by steam hoarder standards (a little less than 500), but sometimes I stumble upon games in my library that I wasn't even aware I had. This was the case with Orwell, and I'm glad that I found this hidden gem.

As a researcher you have to use Orwell (a complex governmental surveillance system) to investigate the lives of multiple citizens of the fictional country "The Nation", and find out those responsible for a series of terror attacks. You can do this by listening to phone calls, reading blog posts, and personal e-mails, hacking laptops, phones and going through medical files, bank records etc. As you make your connections and draw your conclusions you can tailor the story here and there, and you can decide who to incriminate or who to help, but overall your choices do not define the final outcome of the game that much. I liked the atmoshpere and the story has some interesting twists, plus there are multiple endings so it has some replay value as well. Good job Osmotic Studios, this was a very enjoyable experience.

I was happy to find out that there is a sequel to Orwell, I'll definitely buy it in the upcoming months!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I believe Fellow Traveller Games is very interested in making people switch to Tails with giving away their published "Linux basics" game Hacknet for free (multiple times even!) first, and now give away this game too to fuel your paranoia and use some of that know-how to make you try and hide.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.
There is no way to change the font neither through options nor through config files, forum searches gave nothing in regards to that either, so be mindful of that.

Firstly this is a visual novel, so no super exciting and engaging gameplay is to be found, but honestly that may be for the better in these spying games.

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Remember Spycraft: The Great Game? It was this weird mostly live-action-video adventure game that came on 4 cds back in the 90s, and tasked you to roll up an international conspiracy using your wits and a bunch of cool digital tools.

It played off "real" intelligence work, sifting through documents, collecting tidbits of data.

Orwell is a lot like that, but with just the digital shenanigans, played out in an age when the NSA sees you naked and knows who you're gossipping about.

I like it a lot, although it also kinda makes me miss the bits of Spycraft that felt realistic. Like sifting through a document in search of a password or a connection, having to really notice and remember details, and then piecing it all together yourself. 

It worked your brain and engaged you in a way that Orwell doesn't, but Orwell is so well put together that it makes up the difference. It keeps you hooked on the story and the taboo of looking through these peoples lives, sort of tapping into the "Facebook stalker" experience, thinking "God, what a loser" while you're tracing some two-bit musicians path into terrorism.

There are a couple of minor shortcomings though. There's no voice acting on phonecalls, sometimes you find relevant datapoints and you can't use them simply because they don't have "The Outline", and the conflict system can be a bit obtuse, not unlike the Lie/Doubt thing in LA Noire, which is frustrating, but never enough to bring the game down.

So if you want that experience of losing your soul in the service of a faceless controller-state that gives absolutely no fucks about you, then Orwell is about as good as it gets. Happy hunting, you mindless serfs!

Excellent game, thoroughly enjoyed it.  Basically everything would be a spoiler so I'm not going to mention anything game specific, but it plays out like a text-based Telltale game.  Also meta, but not in an obnoxious way - I appreciate that.

As for critiques, it was very irritating to discover information prior to being allowed to select, even when you *know* it is pertinent to the investigation. It felt like too much handholding (with pre-highlighted phrases), and too many bottlenecks stopping me from filling out my investigation at my own pace.  AND LET PLAYERS ZOOM OUT ON THE CONNECTIONS/CONTACTS MAP! It was infuriating scrolling around.  Also, from an intelligence standpoint, the paths to other persons in the contact networks should be labelled with their relationship (Brother, Sister, Girlfriend, etc.) and updated as you discover more information just like everything else. 

Cosmetic Bug: The player can choose which primary profile picture they associate with each person, which changes that picture in all subsequent documents or interactions (calls, texts), but during one scripted cutscene it defaulted to what would probably have been the newest picture I had discovered (Nina in this case) when I had purposely switched to a prior picture. No one would normally notice, but it is still a jarring bug because they were very different pictures and it didn't make logical sense with the way I was building the narrrative for Orwell.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game where you step into the shoes of an "Investigator"; an individual specially chosen outside of the dystopian-like nation simply titled "The Nation" to interact with a big-brother type software that allows you to track and keep tabs on every single person in The Nation. You take control of yourself, your name, your info, you. You've been specially chosen for reasons unknown to yourself or anyone else, per the exception of a secretive few, to be hired at Orwell. Your new "Adviser", Symes, is going to show you the ropes of international and domestic espionage, only this time, you aren't taking down super villians or having a martini "shaken, not stirred" as per the classic spy movie or game, Orwell instead hits close to home....a little too close.

Orwell is a Story Rich, Dystopian, "Choices Matter" Indie game made by Osmotic Studios where you "Investigate the lives of citizens to find those responsible for a series of terror attacks. Information from the internet, personal communications and private files are all accessible to you. But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences.". When Osmotic says that choices matter, they really do. You feel as if you're truly in this dystopian world, helping, or harming, The Nation's citizens. You get to look through countless web pages, trace and listen to countless phone calls, emails, text message and otherwise, even hack into citizen's computers or mobile phones to gain access to information stored on there, such as browsing history, photos, files, and even deleted files. 

For an example (spoiler free); You will be investigating certain citizens, and obviously need to find certain clues about them, their age, phone number, email address, face id, street info, parents, siblings, workplace, links to them from other sources, and you can even go as far as finding medical info from The Nation's hospitals. 

Now let's say I have a citizen I'm investigating, I can start with their relative name, go from there to their social media pages, find out their DOB, address, friends, maybe even mobile number. let's say I need to (or want to) take it further, I begin to suspect they're somehow a threat to The Nation. I can do a little research, Get in contact with friends, trace their calls and emails,  find out information that was never meant to be seen by hacking their computer by getting their PSI address or their IP address, or find ways into their workplace, or even goof off and research their background, what their favourite colour is, or who they're in a relationship with.

Orwell does an amazing job at immersing the investigator (you) into dystopian earth, into The Nation and it's surrounding countries, the citizens who inhabit them and even smaller things like a simple webpage for a local university or a humanitarian organization. Once I started the game, I honestly did not have high expectations nor did I think it was going to be something i was going to enjoy, since it just didn't look or seem like the type of game or genre that i liked, but once i started investigating and learning more about this country, it's citizens and the lore about this world I simply couldn't put it down. I played all the way through, read tons of webpages, information, emails and texts.

That being said, the game is roughly 3-4 hours long, maybe shorter if you (somehow) speedrun it, but if you really want to get immersed into this game world then it can take a lot longer.

[i] And that's not neccesarily a bad thing. [/i]

This is one of a only video game worlds and lore that I genuinly became interested in and invested in as time went on, it truly made me feel like I was impacting the citizens and world around me, mainly because I actually was.

One of the reasons this game resonated with me so much (and one of the reasons I am recommending it) is because in reality, this is not very dystopian. Things like this very well happen in real life and seem so real it's almost disturbing. The amount of dialogue in this game is astonishing, from everything to simple text messages to elaborate corporate emails, everything seems completely geniune, and feels that way too.

Orwell is a masterpeice at storytelling and really making the player truly become immersed and feel like there are consequences. Season 2 of Orwell is coming out sometime soon, and I WILL DEFINETLY be purchasing this game. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes immersive game worlds, spy type games, choice matter games, or just mind-f*ck type games. Absolute great game. 10/10

Oh yeah, this game also takes place in 2017

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In this game, you are the government employee spying on civilians. You read their private posts, listen to their private calls, collect and disseminate information about them, until you have a full picture. It is invasive, horrifying, but might also save lives.
Although, at what cost?

George Orwell and Aldous Huxley would be proud; not in what our society has become, but in what this game truly illustrates what we have learnt from their novels. This is not a university lecture, but a fun game... but at the same time also a game that makes you reflect.
Instead of simply reading about the dangers of how information is used, you get to experience it first-hand, and make your own decisions. Do it well and you prevents horrible things from happening.

But would you be comfortable with powerful - possibly corrupt - governments doing this? Is it worth the danger of being abused?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell:

[h1]Positives:[/h1]

+ The story in this game is great. It covers a goverment project called Orwell, which collects information about citizens. You play as an investigator who is responsible for finding out who committed a series of terrorist attacks. By analysing social media, using phone wire taps and computer hacking, you will pry into the lives of suspects to find the true perpetrator. This is actually really fun and smart. The game does an excellent job of highlighting the problems with mass surveillance too and the plot twists will keep you guessing.

[h1]Negatives:[/h1]

- Because of the low budget, several areas of the game are not as good as they could have been. For example, when "listening" to phone calls via wire-tapping you aren't actually listening to anything - you're reading text which represents each character talking. There's no voice acting in this game at all. A real shame. Furthermore, the digital art sucks. The developers opted for really bizarre suspect photographs in newspapers or social media, which have lots of jagged lines on them. It's hard to explain, but the essence is the pictures in the game look really unrealistic and frankly, silly.

- Most of the game is reading and interacting with the investigator tools given to you. Occasionally you'll receives messages from your government adviser on data chunks you've assembled and their significance. There's literally nothing else in this game. At times it can be a little boring and you just wish there was more creativity, like video footage of potential suspects to review. Something a little different.

- The game is pretty short at about 10 hours. Some limited replayability though.

Overall Score: 7/10

Orwell is not bad, it's actually quite enjoyable. It's fairly basic and there's definitely room for improvement, but I do recommend it. Try to get it for under $5.
